segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: For my presentation today, I’m going to talk about the Ceide Fields in the northwest of Ireland, one of the largest Neolithic sites in the world.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: I recently visited this site and observed the work that is currently being done by a team of archaeologists there.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The site was first discovered in the 1930s by a local teacher, Patrick Caulfield.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: He noticed that when local people were digging in the bog, they were constantly hitting against what seemed to be rows of stones.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: He realised that these must be walls and that they must be thousands of years old for them to predate the bog which subsequently grew over them.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: He wrote to the National Museum in Dublin to ask them to investigate, but no one took him seriously.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: It wasn’t until 40 years later, when Patrick Caulfield’s son Seamus, who had become an archaeologist by then, began to explore further.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: He inserted iron probes into the bog to map the formation of the stones, a traditional method which local people had always used for finding fuel buried in the bog for thousands of years.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Carbon dating later proved that the site was over 5,000 years old and was the largest Neolithic site in Ireland.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Thanks to the bog which covers the area, the remains of the settlement at Ceide Fields, which is over 5,000 years old, are extremely well-preserved.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: A bog is 90 percent water; its soil is so saturated that when the grasses and heathers that grow on its surface die, they don’t fully decay but accumulate in layers.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Objects remain so well preserved in these conditions because of the acidity of the peat and the deficiency of oxygen.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: At least 175 days of rain a year are required for this to happen; this part of Ireland gets an average of 225 days.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The Neolithic farmers at Ceide would have enjoyed several centuries of relative peace and stability.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Neolithic farmers generally lived in larger communities than their predecessors, with a number of houses built around a community building.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: As they lived in permanent settlements, Neolithic farmers were able to build bigger houses.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: These weren’t round as people often assume, but rectangular with a small hole in the roof that allowed smoke to escape.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This is one of many innovations and indicates that the Neolithic farmers were the first people to cook indoors.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Another new technology that Neolithic settlers brought to Ireland was pottery.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Fragments of Neolithic pots have been found in Ceide and elsewhere in Ireland.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The pots were used for many things; as well as for storing food, pots were filled with a small amount of fat and when this was set alight, they served as lamps.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: It’s thought that the Ceide Fields were mainly used as paddocks for animals to graze in.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Evidence from the Ceide Fields suggests that each plot of land was of a suitable size to sustain an extended family.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: They may have used a system of rotational grazing in order to prevent over-grazing and to allow for plant recovery and regrowth.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: This must have been a year-round activity as no structures have been found which would have been used to shelter animals in the winter.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: However, archaeologists believe that this way of life at Ceide ceased abruptly.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Why was this?

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: Well, several factors may have contributed to the changing circumstances.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The soil would have become less productive and led to the abandonment of farming.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The crop rotation system was partly responsible for this as it would have been very intensive and was not sustainable.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: But there were also climatic pressures too.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: The farmers at Ceide would have enjoyed a relatively dry period, but this began to change and the conditions became wetter as there was a lot more rain.

segments.speaker: SPEAKER
segments.en: It was these conditions that encouraged the bog to form over the area which survives today.
